target_audience: University students (Introductory Statistics or Calculus-based Probability)

sections.title: The Bridge: From Counting to Measuring
lecture_lines: Discrete variables count things like Bolt's battery packs.
Continuous variables measure quantities like precise time.
We measure 'how much' instead of 'how many'.
Time and distance can take any value in a range.
This requires a smooth curve instead of bars.
animations: Create 5 blue (#0000FF) battery icons on the left side.
Create a green (#00FF00) stopwatch on the right side with counting decimals.
Fade out the battery icons while scaling up the stopwatch.
The stopwatch decimals extend into a smooth line on the x-axis.
A smooth curve fades in above the line to represent continuity.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Vanishing Histogram
lecture_lines: Histograms show data frequency using rectangular bins.
Narrower bins make the steps look smoother.
As bin width approaches zero, the steps vanish.
The jagged histogram becomes a smooth curve.
This curve is the Probability Density Function.
animations: Create a histogram with 5 wide orange (#FFA500) bars.
Double the number of bars and halve their width.
Repeat the process until bars are very thin lines.
A yellow (#FFFF00) smooth curve appears, tracing the tops of the bars.
Fade out the bars, leaving only the smooth yellow PDF curve.

sections.title: Defining the PDF: Height vs. Area
lecture_lines: The curve f(x) is not the actual probability.
Height f(x) represents the density at a point.
Probability is the area under the curve.
The function f(x) can never be negative.
Total area under the curve must equal one.
animations: Draw a white (#FFFFFF) bell curve on a horizontal axis.
Draw a cyan (#00FFFF) vertical line from x=5 to the curve.
Shade the entire area under the curve in purple (#800080).

sections.title: Calculating Probability: The Integral Slice
lecture_lines: Integration calculates probability for a specific range.
We shade a slice under the curve between points.
Shading from a to b gives the interval's probability.
animations: On a PDF curve, mark points 'a' and 'b' on the x-axis.
Shade the area under the curve between 'a' and 'b' in red (#FF0000).
Display the formula 'P(a < X < b) = Area' in white (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: The Single Point Paradox
lecture_lines: Probability at an exact point is always zero.
A single vertical line has no width.
Zero width means zero area and zero probability.
animations: Place a single red (#FF0000) vertical line at a point on the curve.
Scale the width of the line to 0 to emphasize zero area.
Text 'Area = 0' appears above the line in silver (#C0C0C0).

sections.title: Summary and Application
lecture_lines: We moved from histograms to smooth PDF curves.
PDFs use area to find probability in intervals.
These curves model real-world data like failure times.
animations: Morph the curve between Normal and Exponential distribution shapes.
Shade a small 'danger zone' tail in red (#FF0000) at the end of the curve.
Display the text 'PDF: The Logic of Continuous Data' in gold (#FFD700).
